pairs.rationale: Both passages explicitly describe being compelled to perform service. The instruction about going a Roman mile is compared with Simon being compelled to carry the cross. The cross-bearing account supplies neither a mile distance nor a second-mile response; this is a concrete thematic comparison, not an identification of commands or occasions.

pairs.relationship: thematic parallel: reports following restoration of the dead
pairs.rationale: Both narratives describe a report spreading regionally after the restoration of a dead person. Matthew closes the raising of the girl with a report throughout the land; Luke describes the young man being raised and the report spreading through Judea and the surrounding region. These are corresponding narrative effects in different episodes, not the same incident.

pairs.relationship: same-book structural parallel: completed teaching and departure
pairs.rationale: Both notices use the completion of Jesus' teaching to introduce His moving on. One follows the directions to the Twelve and leads to teaching and proclaiming in their cities; the other follows the parables. This compares an explicit internal transition pattern without identifying the journeys as one occasion.

pairs.relationship: same-book structural parallel: completed teaching and departure
pairs.rationale: Both sentences say that Jesus finished a block of teaching and then departed. Matthew 13 closes the parables; Matthew 19 closes the preceding words and names the move from Galilee toward Judea beyond the Jordan. The shared discourse-closing and departure pattern is an internal literary connection, not independent testimony or an identical journey.

deferred.reason: The actual Matthew lineage was reread beside Luke 3:23–24 and the postexilic families in 1 Chronicles 3:19–24. Those records do not establish this Azor–Zadok–Achim–Eliud chain; similarly situated or repeated names cannot settle these identities. No pair is retained.

The Matthew chain was reconsidered with Luke 3:23–24 and 1 Chronicles 3:19–24. Neither supplied passage attests the Eliud–Eleazar–Matthan–Jacob chain. No identity or relationship is manufactured from similar names.

Matthew 5:17 and 21:32 were reread with the baptismal exchange. They concern fulfillment and John's righteous way, but do not explain Jesus permitting this baptism to fulfill all righteousness. The distinctive exchange remains without a retained counterpart.

The almsgiving instruction and its secrecy image were reconsidered in Matthew 6:1–4. The surrounding reward language does not independently reproduce the left-hand/right-hand image, so repeating neighboring context would not resolve this deferred unit.

The grooming instructions were reconsidered beside 2 Samuel 12:20 and its fasting context. David washes and anoints after his fast; Matthew commands ordinary appearance while fasting. That limited overlap does not establish a close counterpart to this particular fasting instruction.

Luke 6:17 was reread as a candidate because it describes descent and a crowd. Its distinct level-place scene does not supply a sufficiently specific counterpart to Matthew's transition after the mountain teaching. No identity of occasion or completion is claimed.

The warning about uprooting wheat while gathering darnel was reread with the later explanation in Matthew 13:37–43. The explanation identifies the plants and harvest but not this hazard of premature removal. The warning remains deferred.

The scribe-householder comparison was reread with the surrounding parable conclusions. A generic overlap involving treasure or old/new possessions does not establish its particular claim about a scribe made a kingdom disciple. No unsupported allusion is retained.

Mark 6:38–39 was reread with the feeding context. It records counting the loaves and arranging the people, without Jesus' particular command to bring the food to Him. Shared feeding context alone does not resolve this individual unit.

Peter's request was reconsidered beside John 21:4–7. The later shore scene has recognition of the Lord, but no corresponding request to be commanded onto the waters. The episodes and the distinctive request are not conflated.

John 21:4–7 was reread as a possible Peter-and-sea comparison. It describes Peter throwing himself into the sea after hearing that it is the Lord, not walking on it at Jesus' command. The limited shared setting was not retained as a sufficiently precise counterpart to this action.

The offense report was reread with Mark 7:17 and its discourse context. Mark records the disciples asking in the house, not their report of the Pharisees' offense. A generic shared response to teaching does not resolve the stated report.

Mark 7:24–30 was reread in full beside the woman's approach. It does not reproduce Jesus' initial silence or the disciples' request to dismiss her. No correspondence for those distinctive actions is credited.

Exodus 30:13–15 was reread. Its actual wording gives half a didrachma for the census contribution, while Matthew speaks of the didrachmas collectors. The texts alone do not establish the levy's identity or amount; the proposed equivalence remains unresolved.

The question was reread with the full Matthew 17:24–27 tax exchange and Exodus 30:13–15. The census contribution does not supply Jesus' sons-versus-strangers analogy about earthly kings. General tax vocabulary is insufficient.

The conclusion was reconsidered in the immediate royal-tax analogy. General spiritual-freedom sayings would not reproduce the specific sons-versus-strangers reasoning. No equivalence between those different arguments is retained.

The fellow servants' grief and report were reconsidered in Matthew 18:23–35. Neighboring responses explain the narrative but do not provide a separate precise counterpart to the report. It remains deferred without duplicating generic grief/reporting notices.

1 Corinthians 7:1 and 7:8–9 were reread as candidates. Paul's qualified advice to the unmarried and widows does not reproduce the disciples' reaction to the divorce instruction. Their reaction is not silently converted into Paul's counsel.

The third-hour hiring detail was reread in the full Matthew 20:1–16 hiring narrative. Its exact time and marketplace action lack an established independent counterpart; another round of the same story is not used to create completion.

The sixth- and ninth-hour hiring rounds were reconsidered in Matthew 20:1–16. Repetition within this single hiring sequence does not independently establish a precise cross-reference for these time details.
The eleventh-hour question was reread with the full hiring sequence. No precise counterpart to the time and all-day-idleness question is established; broad vineyard or work imagery earns no credit.

The un-hired workers' explanation and invitation were reconsidered in the complete hiring narrative. The generic invitation to work does not supply a precise independent counterpart to their stated reason and response.

The king's inspection was reread with Matthew 22:1–14. General clothing images do not establish what this wedding garment represents or independently reproduce the inspection. No allegorical identity is asserted.
The garment question and speechless response were reconsidered in Matthew 22:1–14. Neither generic garment symbolism nor an unrelated silence establishes a precise counterpart to this exchange.

1 Peter 2:9 was reread as a called/chosen candidate. It identifies a chosen people called out of darkness, without Matthew's many/few distinction. Shared vocabulary alone was not credited, and no unavailable Revelation text was invented.

review_notes: All 29 previously deferred Matthew units were substantively reread with local context and the named actual candidate passages. Four new limited passage-grounded connections are proposed; 25 cases remain without completion credit.
The two internal transition pairs concern the explicit completed-teaching/departure pattern. They do not treat separate travel events as one incident.
No original source wording, IDs, continuation paragraphs or numerical gaps were changed. Revisited units are separated from first-read source counts.
